whyChoose.title: What California Law Means for Your Claim

items.title: A Filing Clock That Won't Wait
items.desc: California generally gives you two years from the date of injury to file a personal injury claim. If a government vehicle or roadway was involved, that window can shrink to as little as six months, so timing matters.

items.title: Being Partly at Fault Doesn't End Your Claim
items.desc: Under California's pure comparative fault rule, you can still recover damages even if you were partly responsible for the crash. Your compensation is simply reduced by your share of fault, not eliminated.

items.title: No Ceiling on Pain and Suffering
items.desc: California places no cap on non-economic damages, like pain and suffering, in typical injury cases. This can matter significantly if your injury has affected your daily life beyond medical bills.

items.title: You Pay Nothing Upfront
items.desc: We work on contingency, meaning we only get paid if you receive a settlement or award. There's no retainer and no hourly bill to worry about while you focus on recovering.

items.question: How much does it cost to talk to us?
items.answer: Nothing. Our initial consultation is free, and there's no obligation to move forward. If we take your case, we work on contingency, so you don't pay unless there's a recovery.

items.question: How long do I have to file a claim in California?
items.answer: In most personal injury cases, California law gives you two years from the date of the incident. If your injury involved a government entity or vehicle, that deadline can be as short as six months, so it's worth reaching out sooner rather than later.

items.question: What if I was partly responsible for the accident?
items.answer: California follows a pure comparative fault rule, which means you can still recover compensation even if you share some blame. Your total award would be reduced by your percentage of fault, but it wouldn't be barred entirely.

items.question: Where do crashes tend to cluster in Arroyo Grande?
items.answer: Public crash records show higher collision counts along US-101 Southbound, E Grand Avenue, US-101 Northbound, and El Camino Real. These are simply the corridors with the most reported collisions, not a judgment about any particular stretch of road.
